q: What is asynchronous Apex and why do we use it?
alt: What do you mean by async Apex?
Why would you run Apex in the background?
What are the different types of asynchronous Apex?
explain a sink apex in salesforce
a: Async Apex is how I keep slow work out of the user's save. It's code that runs later, in its own separate transaction, when the platform has resources free, so the user doesn't sit there waiting. I reach for it for three reasons. One, long-running work like processing big data volumes. Two, callouts, because they can't run in the same context as DML or straight from a trigger. Three, higher governor limits: async gets 200 SOQL queries, 12 MB heap and 60 seconds of CPU. Say a user saves an Opportunity and we need to send it to an ERP system. Instead of making them wait on that call, I hand it to an async job and the save finishes right away. There are four types: future methods, Queueable Apex, Batch Apex and Scheduled Apex. Platform Events are also often used to decouple work asynchronously. When I explain it to a business user, I put it simply: the save is instant, and the heavy lifting finishes a few seconds later.
points: Runs in its own transaction, user does not wait
Higher limits: 200 SOQL, 12 MB heap, 60 s CPU
Types: future, Queueable, Batch, Schedulable
Common uses: callouts, large data, mixed DML fixes

q: What is a future method and what are its rules?
alt: How do you write an @future method?
What are the limitations of future methods?
Explain the future annotation in Apex
rules for at future method
a: Future methods are fine for small fire-and-forget work, but I treat them as the simplest tool, not the default. A future method is a static method marked @future that Salesforce runs asynchronously in its own transaction. The rules: it must be static and return void, and parameters can only be primitives, arrays or collections of primitives. So I pass record Ids, not sObjects, and re-query inside. For example, if a trigger needs to update the rating on 20 Accounts in the background, I pass the Set of 20 Account Ids, and the future method queries them fresh and updates them. A few more limits. You can't call a future method from another future method or from Batch Apex. There's no job Id returned, so you can't monitor or chain it, and the execution order isn't guaranteed. You can call up to 50 future methods per transaction. And if it makes a callout, I add callout=true. Because there's no job Id or chaining, on my teams new async code usually goes to a Queueable instead.
points: static void, primitives only (pass Ids)
Cannot be called from future or batch
No job Id, no chaining, order not guaranteed
50 future calls per transaction

q: You need to call an external API whenever a record is created. Can you do the callout from the trigger?
alt: How do you make a callout from a trigger?
Can we do a callout directly from a trigger?
Write a future method with callout equals true
Callout from trigger gives an error, how do you fix it?
how to call external API when record is created
a: No, you can't make a synchronous callout from a trigger. The trigger runs inside the database transaction, and Salesforce won't let that transaction sit and wait on an external system. So I move the callout to async code. The classic way is a future method with callout=true that takes the record Ids, re-queries them and makes the HTTP request. These days I prefer a Queueable that implements Database.AllowsCallouts, because I can pass more data, get a job Id, and chain or retry. Say a data load inserts 50 Accounts and each one has to go to a billing system. In code review, the thing I check first is that the trigger enqueues once for all 50 records together, not 50 separate jobs. One enqueue, one set of Ids, for the whole trigger batch.
points: Synchronous callouts are not allowed in triggers
Use @future(callout=true) or Queueable with Database.AllowsCallouts
Enqueue once per trigger batch, not per record

q: What is Queueable Apex?
alt: Explain the Queueable interface
How do you write a queueable class?
What is System.enqueueJob?
what is q able apex
a: Queueable is my default for new async work. It's a class that implements the Queueable interface and its execute method, and I start it with System.enqueueJob. I think of it as a future method with more power. It can hold complex member variables like sObjects or wrapper classes. enqueueJob returns a job Id that I can track in AsyncApexJob. And I can chain another job from execute. For example, I can pass a list of Opportunity records straight into the Queueable's constructor, enqueue it, and keep the job Id so I can check its status later. You can't do any of that with a future method. It also supports callouts with Database.AllowsCallouts, and Transaction Finalizers for failure handling. The limit to remember: up to 50 enqueueJob calls in a synchronous transaction, but only one from inside an executing Queueable. That's the limit I plan around when someone designs a chain.
points: Implements Queueable, method execute(QueueableContext)
Accepts complex types, returns a job Id
Supports chaining, callouts and finalizers
50 enqueueJob per sync transaction, 1 from an async one

q: How do you chain Queueable jobs?
alt: Can a queueable call another queueable?
How to run jobs one after another in Apex?
Explain queueable chaining with an example
how many jobs can I chain from queueable
a: I chain only when step two genuinely depends on step one. To chain, I call System.enqueueJob for the next job at the end of the current job's execute method. Each running Queueable can add only one child job, so the chain is a straight line, one job after another. That's useful when step two depends on step one. For example, job one creates the invoices, and only when it's done does it enqueue job two, which emails them out. In production there's no limit on chain depth, but in Developer and Trial orgs it's capped at five jobs, including the parent. A stop condition is non-negotiable in review, so the chain doesn't run forever. And in test context I guard the chaining with Test.isRunningTest or a flag, because older docs say chaining inside a test throws an error, and current docs only support it with an appropriate stack depth.
points: Enqueue the next job inside execute
Only one child job per executing Queueable
No depth limit in production; 5 in Developer/Trial orgs
Always add a stop condition

q: What is a Transaction Finalizer in Queueable Apex?
alt: How do you handle failures in a queueable job?
Explain System.Finalizer interface
How do you retry a failed queueable?
what is attach finalizer
a: I'd attach a finalizer to any Queueable that matters to the business, because it's the only reliable way to catch a hard failure. A Transaction Finalizer is a class that implements System.Finalizer, and it runs after a Queueable job finishes, whether the job succeeded or failed with an unhandled exception, even an uncatchable one like a limit exception. I attach it inside execute with System.attachFinalizer. In the finalizer's execute, I check FinalizerContext.getResult, which is SUCCESS or UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION, and getException gives me the error. Say a Queueable syncing orders blows the CPU limit. Normally that failure just disappears. With a finalizer, I can log it to a custom object, notify someone, or re-enqueue the job as a retry. A few limits to remember: only one finalizer per job, it can enqueue one async job, and a failed job can be re-enqueued by its finalizer up to five times in a row. So the retry logic needs a cap, which I make sure is there before it ships.
points: Implements System.Finalizer, attached with System.attachFinalizer
Runs on success and on unhandled failure
Use for logging, alerts and retries
One finalizer per job; re-enqueue up to 5 consecutive times

q: How do you delay a Queueable job or set AsyncOptions?
alt: Can I schedule a queueable to run after a few minutes?
What is AsyncOptions in Apex?
How to add a delay to System.enqueueJob?
set max stack depth for queueable
a: For rate-limited integrations, I'd use a delayed enqueue rather than hammering the API. System.enqueueJob has an overload that takes a delay in minutes, from zero to ten, so the job won't start before that delay. That's handy for retry with back-off, or when an external system is rate-limiting you. Say an API sends back a "too many requests" error. I can re-enqueue the job with a five-minute delay instead of hitting it again right away. There's also an AsyncOptions class where I can set MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes, MaximumQueueableStackDepth to cap how deep a chain can go, and a DuplicateSignature so the same job isn't queued twice. Inside the job, the AsyncInfo class tells me the current stack depth. One gotcha: the delay is ignored in test context, so my tests don't rely on it. I set the delay and stack-depth values as team standards per integration, so nobody hard-codes their own.
points: enqueueJob(job, delayMinutes) with 0 to 10 minutes
AsyncOptions: delay, max stack depth, duplicate signature
AsyncInfo.getCurrentQueueableStackDepth()
Delay is ignored in tests

q: How do you prevent the same Queueable job from being enqueued twice?
alt: How to avoid duplicate queueable jobs for the same record?
What is QueueableDuplicateSignature?
Two triggers are queuing the same job, how do you dedupe?
a: My answer is a duplicate signature, not home-made checks. I attach a duplicate signature to the Queueable through AsyncOptions. I build it with QueueableDuplicateSignature.Builder, adding values like the record Id and the job name, and pass the options to System.enqueueJob. If a job with the same signature is already waiting in the queue, the next enqueue throws a DuplicateMessageException, which I catch and ignore. For example, say three quick updates hit the same Account and each one tries to queue a sync job. With a signature built from that Account Id, only the first gets queued and the other two are skipped. One catch: the signature is removed once a job starts running, so it doesn't block a duplicate of a job that's already running. This cuts down lock contention and race conditions. Before this feature, people checked AsyncApexJob or used a static flag, which is less reliable. When I see those older patterns in review, I ask whether a signature would do the job more cleanly.
points: Use AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature
Build with QueueableDuplicateSignature.Builder
Duplicate enqueue throws DuplicateMessageException
Reduces race conditions and lock contention

q: What is Batch Apex and what are its methods?
alt: Explain the Database.Batchable interface
What are start, execute and finish in batch?
How does batch apex work?
bach apex methods
a: When the volume is too big for one transaction, I go to Batch Apex. It's for processing large numbers of records, even millions, by splitting them into chunks. The class implements Database.Batchable with three methods. Start runs once and returns the records to process, as a QueryLocator or an Iterable. Execute runs once per chunk, 200 records by default, and each chunk is its own transaction with fresh governor limits. Finish runs once at the end, and I use it to send a summary email or chain the next job. For example, if I need to update 50,000 Contact records, start returns the query, execute runs 250 times with 200 records each, and finish emails me the result. I kick it off with Database.executeBatch, which returns the job Id. On my teams, every batch also has to be safe to re-run, because that's what saves you when a chunk fails at 2 AM.
points: start: collect records (QueryLocator or Iterable)
execute: process each chunk, default 200
finish: post-processing, emails, chaining
Each chunk gets fresh governor limits

q: What is Database.Stateful in Batch Apex?
alt: How do you maintain state across batch chunks?
Why are my batch variables resetting in every execute?
When should you use Database.Stateful?
data base stateful interface
a: I use Database.Stateful only when I genuinely need totals or Ids across chunks. By default Batch Apex is stateless. Each execute call gets a fresh copy of the class, so instance variables reset between chunks. If I implement Database.Stateful, instance variables keep their values across all execute calls and are still there in finish. Say I'm updating 10,000 records and want to email a summary like "9,950 succeeded, 50 failed." Without Stateful, my counters go back to zero every chunk. With it, they keep adding up, and finish can send the totals. The trade-off is that the state is serialized after every chunk, which adds time and counts toward heap. So I keep it small, like counts and Ids, not full record lists. And static variables are never kept across chunks. If I see a full record list held in a Stateful batch during review, that's a heap risk I'd ask to change.
points: Stateless by default: instance variables reset per chunk
Stateful keeps instance variables across execute and finish
Serialization cost; keep state small
Static variables are not preserved

q: What is the difference between QueryLocator and Iterable in Batch Apex?
alt: When would you return an Iterable from start?
QueryLocator vs Iterable in batch start method
How many records can a batch process with QueryLocator?
query locator versus iterable
a: My default is QueryLocator, and the team needs a reason to pick anything else. It's based on a single SOQL query and lets the batch process up to 50 million records, because the 50,000 query-row limit doesn't apply in start. An Iterable is for when the records don't come from one simple query, like combining data from several objects, a list built in code, or results from a callout. The catch is that with an Iterable, normal governor limits apply in start, so any SOQL there is still capped at 50,000 rows. So if I need to clean up 2 million old Task records, that's a QueryLocator. If I'm building a custom list by merging two queries with a callout response, that's an Iterable. Large volume on one object, QueryLocator. Custom logic, Iterable.
points: QueryLocator: one SOQL query, up to 50 million records
Iterable: custom source, normal limits apply in start
Iterable SOQL still capped at 50,000 rows
Default to QueryLocator for large data

q: What is the batch size in Batch Apex and how do you change it?
alt: What is the default scope size for batch?
Maximum batch size in Salesforce?
How do you pass scope to Database.executeBatch?
why would I reduce batch size
a: I treat batch size as a tuning decision, not a constant. The default scope is 200 records per execute, and I can pass a second parameter to Database.executeBatch to change it, from 1 up to 2,000 with a QueryLocator. Larger chunks mean fewer transactions and faster overall runs, but each chunk has more work, so it can hit CPU, heap or DML limits. I reduce the scope when each record triggers heavy logic, when I make a callout per record, or when I see row-lock errors. For example, a batch doing one callout per record might use a scope of 50 or even 1, while a simple field update can use 2,000. I'd rather the scope sit in custom metadata, so we can tune it in production without a deployment.
points: Default 200, maximum 2,000 for QueryLocator
Second argument of Database.executeBatch
Smaller scope for heavy logic, callouts, lock errors
Larger scope for simple, fast updates

q: What happens if one chunk of a batch job fails?
alt: If execute throws an exception, do other chunks roll back?
Does batch apex roll back all records on error?
Is batch apex all or nothing?
a: The short answer is only that chunk rolls back. Batch Apex isn't all-or-nothing across the whole job. Each execute call is its own transaction. So if one chunk throws an unhandled exception, only that chunk's changes roll back. Chunks that already finished stay committed, and the rest keep running. The failed chunk shows up in NumberOfErrors on AsyncApexJob. Say I run a batch over 1,000 records in chunks of 200, and chunk three fails. Chunks one and two are saved, chunks four and five still run, and only those 200 records in chunk three roll back. Inside a chunk, though, if I use plain update with the default all-or-none behaviour, one bad record fails the whole chunk. That's why I usually use Database.update with allOrNone false, log the failed rows, and make the job re-runnable so a second run only picks up unfinished records. That re-run plan is what I explain to stakeholders up front, so a partial failure isn't a surprise.
points: Each chunk is a separate transaction
Only the failing chunk rolls back
NumberOfErrors on AsyncApexJob shows failed chunks
Use partial success and make the job re-runnable

q: How do you monitor a batch or async job?
alt: How do I check the status of a batch job?
What is AsyncApexJob?
Where can I see running batch jobs?
query async apex job status
a: My rule is that nobody should have to go looking for a failed job; it should tell us. I monitor async jobs in two ways. In Setup, there's the Apex Jobs page, which shows status, total batches, batches processed and failures, and the Apex Flex Queue page for jobs waiting to run. In code, I query the AsyncApexJob object using the job Id that executeBatch or enqueueJob returned. The key fields are Status, like Queued, Processing, Completed, Failed or Aborted, plus JobItemsProcessed, TotalJobItems, NumberOfErrors, and ExtendedStatus for the first error. For example, in a batch's finish method I often query its own AsyncApexJob record and send an email saying something like "48 of 50 batches processed, 2 errors," with the first error taken from ExtendedStatus. That way nobody has to go and check Setup.
points: Setup: Apex Jobs and Apex Flex Queue pages
Query AsyncApexJob by job Id
Status, JobItemsProcessed, TotalJobItems, NumberOfErrors
ExtendedStatus shows the first error

q: What is the Apex Flex Queue?
alt: What happens when I submit more than five batch jobs?
Explain holding status in batch jobs
How many batch jobs can run at the same time?
flex queue in salesforce
a: The Flex Queue is the overflow line for batch jobs. Only five batch jobs can be actively queued or processing at the same time. The Apex Flex Queue lets you submit more than that. Extra batch jobs go into the flex queue with a status of Holding, and it can hold up to 100 jobs. As slots free up, Salesforce moves jobs from the flex queue into the active queue, in order. Say I submit eight batch jobs at once. Five go active, and the other three sit in the flex queue as Holding until a slot opens. Admins can reorder or cancel holding jobs from the Apex Flex Queue page in Setup. In Apex, the FlexQueue class has methods to move a job to the front or behind another job. And if the flex queue is full, executeBatch throws an exception. So when several teams share an org, I keep an eye on how many nightly batches we're all submitting at once.
points: 5 concurrent active batch jobs
Flex queue holds up to 100 jobs in Holding status
Reorder in Setup or with the FlexQueue class
Full queue causes executeBatch to fail

q: How do you abort a running batch or scheduled job?
alt: How to stop a batch job in Salesforce?
How do you delete a scheduled apex job?
What is System.abortJob?
cancel running apex job
a: To stop a job, I use System.abortJob and pass the job Id. For a batch or Queueable, the Id comes from AsyncApexJob. For a scheduled job, I pass the CronTrigger Id, which System.schedule returns. Admins can also click Abort on the Apex Jobs page, or Delete on the Scheduled Jobs page in Setup. One thing to know: aborting a batch stops further chunks, but chunks that already committed are not rolled back. So if a batch is halfway through, the first half stays updated. The other gotcha shows up at deployment. Say I need to change a class that runs on a nightly schedule. Salesforce blocks changes to classes with pending scheduled jobs, unless deployment with active jobs is allowed. So I usually abort the scheduled job first, deploy, and then schedule it again. That abort and reschedule step goes into our release checklist, so it isn't left to memory.
points: System.abortJob(jobId)
Batch/Queueable: AsyncApexJob Id; scheduled: CronTrigger Id
Committed chunks are not rolled back
Abort scheduled jobs before changing their class

q: What is Scheduled Apex and how do you write it?
alt: Explain the Schedulable interface
How do you schedule Apex to run daily?
Write a schedulable class
how to schedule apex class
a: I keep Scheduled Apex as a thin trigger for the real work. Scheduled Apex lets a class run at a specific time or on a recurring schedule. The class implements the Schedulable interface, with one method, execute, that takes a SchedulableContext. I can schedule it two ways. From Setup, using Schedule Apex, which allows weekly runs on chosen days or monthly runs at a preferred start time. Or in code, with System.schedule and a cron expression, for more control. Best practice, and my standard on the team, is to keep the scheduled class thin. For example, my nightly cleanup class does nothing in execute except call Database.executeBatch on the real cleanup batch. All the logic lives in the batch or Queueable. And remember the limit: an org can have up to 100 scheduled Apex jobs at one time.
points: Implements Schedulable, execute(SchedulableContext)
Schedule from Setup or System.schedule with cron
Keep it thin; start a batch or Queueable
Up to 100 scheduled Apex jobs per org

q: Explain cron expressions in System.schedule.
alt: How do you write a cron expression for Salesforce?
Schedule a job at 2 AM every day using cron
What are the fields in a Salesforce cron expression?
chron expression apex
a: Cron is what gives System.schedule its precision. System.schedule takes three arguments: a unique job name, a cron expression, and an instance of the Schedulable class. It returns the CronTrigger Id. A Salesforce cron expression has six or seven fields in this order: seconds, minutes, hours, day of month, month, day of week, and an optional year. A question mark means no specific value and is used in either day of month or day of week. So zero zero two star star question mark means 2 AM every day, and zero zero nine question mark star MON-FRI means 9 AM on weekdays. Seconds and minutes must be fixed values, so cron cannot run more often than once an hour. In review, I ask for the cron string to have a plain-English comment next to it, because these are easy to misread.
points: Seconds Minutes Hours Day-of-month Month Day-of-week [Year]
'?' used in day-of-month or day-of-week
System.schedule returns the CronTrigger Id
For more frequent runs, schedule several jobs

q: Can you make a callout from Scheduled Apex?
alt: Callout from schedulable class throws an error, why?
How to call an API on a schedule?
Synchronous callouts from scheduled apex
a: Not directly, so I design around it. Synchronous callouts aren't supported from the execute method of a Schedulable class. The standard fix is to have the scheduled class start something that does support callouts. That's a Batch class that implements Database.AllowsCallouts, a Queueable that implements Database.AllowsCallouts, or a future method with callout=true. For example, for a nightly sync of Accounts to an external system, I schedule a batch with callouts, so I get chunking and retry handling. For one small request, like pulling a single file of rates every morning, a Queueable started from the scheduler is enough. The trade-off I weigh is volume: batch for many records, Queueable for one quick call.
points: No synchronous callouts in Schedulable.execute
Start a Queueable or Batch with Database.AllowsCallouts
Or call a future method with callout=true

q: What are Platform Events?
alt: Explain platform events in Salesforce
What is event-driven architecture in Salesforce?
Why use platform events instead of a direct callout?
plat form events use case
a: I use Platform Events when I want systems to talk without depending on each other. They're Salesforce's publish-subscribe messaging. I define an event like an object, with the __e suffix and custom fields. Publishers send event messages and subscribers react to them, and neither side knows about the other. Publishers can be Apex, Flow, or external systems through the API. Subscribers can be Apex triggers, Flows, LWC using the empApi module, or external systems through the Pub/Sub API or CometD. Say an order gets marked as shipped. I publish an Order_Shipped__e event, a Flow picks it up and emails the customer, and a warehouse system picks up the same event through the Pub/Sub API. The publisher doesn't care who's listening. I use them to decouple systems, to integrate with external apps in near real time, and to log errors that must survive a rollback.
points: Publish/subscribe, object with __e suffix
Publish from Apex, Flow or API
Subscribe with triggers, Flow, LWC empApi, Pub/Sub API
Decouples publishers and subscribers

q: How do you publish a Platform Event from Apex?
alt: Write code to publish a platform event
What is EventBus.publish?
How do you know if a platform event was published successfully?
a: Publishing is simple, but the team has to understand what success really means. I create instances of the event object, set the fields, and call EventBus.publish with a single event or a list. It returns Database.SaveResult objects, so I loop through them and check isSuccess and getErrors. The gotcha: a successful result means the publish request was queued, not that subscribers have processed it, because delivery is asynchronous. And publishing inside a loop is something I flag in every review; we publish a list in one call. For example, if 100 Orders ship in one transaction, I build a list of 100 events and call EventBus.publish once. Whether the events go out immediately or only after the transaction commits depends on the Publish Behavior setting on the event definition.
points: EventBus.publish(list) returns SaveResults
Success means queued, delivery is async
Publish in bulk, not in a loop
Publish Behavior setting controls timing

q: How do you subscribe to a Platform Event with an Apex trigger?
alt: Write a trigger on a platform event
What events does a platform event trigger support?
Which user runs the platform event trigger?
platform event subscriber in apex
a: I subscribe with an after insert trigger on the event object, because after insert is the only event supported. The trigger runs asynchronously in its own transaction, by default as the Automated Process user. It gets events in batches of up to 2,000, not 200 like normal triggers, so the code has to be fully bulkified. A query inside a loop over 2,000 events will fail fast. Because the running user is Automated Process, records it creates are owned by that user, unless I configure a different running user. That surprises people, for example when new Cases from the trigger show up owned by Automated Process. Debug logs also need a trace flag on that user. Both the batch size and the running user can be changed with PlatformEventSubscriberConfig. I make sure that running user is decided up front, because ownership and sharing issues are hard to fix after go-live.
points: Only after insert is supported
Batches of up to 2,000 events
Runs as Automated Process user by default
Configure via PlatformEventSubscriberConfig

q: What is the difference between Publish Immediately and Publish After Commit?
alt: Platform event publish behavior options
Can a published platform event be rolled back?
How do you log errors with platform events even if the transaction fails?
a: My rule is After Commit for business events and Immediately for error logs. This is a setting on the platform event definition. With Publish After Commit, the event is published only if the transaction commits successfully, so if the transaction rolls back, the event is never sent, and setSavepoint and rollback apply to it. That is what I want for business events like Order Shipped, so subscribers never act on data that does not exist. With Publish Immediately, the event goes out as soon as publish is called, regardless of the transaction outcome, and it cannot be rolled back. That is perfect for error logging: I publish a log event in a catch block, and it survives even when the main transaction fails. Getting this choice wrong is a quiet bug, so I check the setting on every new event in review.
points: After Commit: only sent if the transaction commits
Immediately: sent right away, cannot be rolled back
Business events: After Commit
Error logging: Immediately

q: What is the Replay ID and how long are Platform Events retained?
alt: How can a subscriber get missed events?
Explain replay id in platform events
What is the retention for high volume platform events?
how to replay events in salesforce
a: Replay is what makes event integrations recoverable, so I plan for it from day one. Every event message gets a Replay ID, a sequence value that lets a subscriber resume from a point in the event stream. High-volume platform events, which is the default for new events, are stored on the event bus for 72 hours. Say an external system on the Pub/Sub API goes down overnight for maintenance. When it comes back, it reconnects with the last Replay ID it processed and gets everything it missed, as long as it's within those 72 hours. It can also replay from the earliest stored event. One gotcha: Replay IDs aren't guaranteed to be contiguous, so I never treat them as a gap-free counter. Legacy standard-volume events have shorter retention, and Salesforce has announced their retirement, so I always use high-volume events. I also tell the integration team plainly that 72 hours is their recovery window, so their outage plan fits inside it.
points: Replay ID marks position in the event stream
High-volume events retained for 72 hours
Subscribers resume from last processed Replay ID
Replay IDs are not contiguous

q: How do you handle errors and retries in a Platform Event trigger?
alt: My platform event trigger failed halfway, how do I resume?
What is EventBus.RetryableException?
Explain setResumeCheckpoint in platform event triggers
a: I'd use two tools together, and I expect both in any event trigger my team ships. First, setResumeCheckpoint. As I process each event, I call EventBus.TriggerContext.currentContext().setResumeCheckpoint with that event's ReplayId. If the trigger then hits a limit or exception, the next invocation resumes after the last checkpoint, so already-processed events aren't repeated. Say the trigger gets 500 events and fails on number 301. With checkpoints, the next run starts at 301, not back at 1. Second, if the failure is temporary, like a locked record, I can throw EventBus.RetryableException. Salesforce then re-fires the trigger with the same batch of events after a delay, for a limited number of retries. I combine both with logging, so events that keep failing are captured and not silently lost.
points: setResumeCheckpoint(replayId) to resume after the last good event
Throw EventBus.RetryableException for transient failures
Retries are limited, so log permanent failures

q: What is Change Data Capture?
alt: Explain CDC in Salesforce
How do external systems get notified when records change?
Write a trigger on a change event
change data capture use case
a: When an external system needs to mirror Salesforce data, CDC is my first choice, because nobody has to write publishing code. Change Data Capture publishes change events automatically whenever records of a selected object are created, updated, deleted or undeleted. I just enable the object on the Change Data Capture setup page, and Salesforce publishes events like AccountChangeEvent, with no code on the publishing side. Each event has a ChangeEventHeader with the change type, the record Ids, and the list of changed fields, so subscribers get only what changed. For example, if a rep updates just the Phone on an Account, the event says UPDATE, gives that Account Id, and lists Phone as the changed field. External systems subscribe through the Pub/Sub API to keep their copy in sync. Inside Salesforce, I can also write an after insert Apex trigger on the change event for async processing. Events are retained for three days, which is the recovery window I build the subscriber's catch-up plan around.
points: Enable per object in Setup, no publish code
Events like AccountChangeEvent
ChangeEventHeader: changeType, recordIds, changedFields
Used to sync external systems in near real time

q: What is the difference between Platform Events and Change Data Capture?
alt: When to use CDC vs platform events?

a: I decide this by asking one question: are we replicating data, or announcing a business event? Both run on the same event bus, but they solve different needs. Change Data Capture is about data changes. Salesforce publishes events automatically for every create, update, delete and undelete on the objects I enable, with the changed fields included, and I can't add custom fields to the event. It's ideal for keeping an external database or data warehouse in sync. Platform Events are custom business events that I define and publish myself, like Order Shipped or Payment Failed, with whatever fields I need, and I control exactly when they fire. Say a data warehouse needs a copy of every Account change. That's CDC, with no code. But if a billing system needs to know a payment failed, along with the reason, I'd publish a Payment Failed platform event. Replicating data, CDC. Business processes and integration messages, Platform Events.

Platform Events: custom schema, published by me

q: When would you use future, Queueable, Batch or Scheduled Apex?
alt: How do you choose the right asynchronous option?
Which async apex should I use for my requirement?
Compare all the async apex types
difference between future queueable batch and schedulable
a: I pick based on volume, complexity and timing, and I'd like the whole team using the same decision rule so the codebase stays consistent. A future method is fine for a quick, simple task, like one callout from a trigger, with only primitive parameters. Queueable is my default for most async work. It takes complex data, returns a job Id, supports chaining and finalizers, and is good up to a few thousand records. Batch Apex is for large volumes, tens of thousands to millions of records, because it chunks the work and each chunk gets fresh limits. Scheduled Apex is about timing, running something at a set time, and usually it just kicks off a batch or Queueable. Platform Events fit when I want to decouple publishers from subscribers. So, for example, recalculating a field on 2 million Contacts every Sunday night would be a scheduled class that starts a batch.

q: You get a MIXED_DML_OPERATION error. How do you fix it?
alt: How do you fix mixed DML error?
Insert user and account in the same transaction error
What causes mixed DML operation exception?

a: I fix it by splitting the setup and non-setup work into separate transactions. Mixed DML happens when one transaction does DML on a setup object, like User, Group, GroupMember or PermissionSetAssignment, and also on a non-setup object like Account or a custom object. Salesforce blocks this because setup changes can affect sharing. The fix is to split the work into separate transactions: I do one part synchronously and move the other into an async job, usually a Queueable or a future method. For example, after creating a Contact, I assign a permission set in a Queueable. In test classes, I wrap the setup DML inside System.runAs, which puts it in a separate context. When I review user-provisioning code, this is one of the first things I look for.

q: How are governor limits different for asynchronous Apex?
alt: What limits increase in async apex?
Async vs sync governor limits
Why does my code work in batch but fail in a trigger?
a: Async gives you more headroom, but it's not a fix for bad code. Async transactions get higher limits on the ones people hit most. SOQL queries go from 100 to 200, heap from 6 MB to 12 MB, and maximum CPU time from 10 seconds to 60. Many other limits stay the same, though: 150 DML statements, 10,000 DML rows, 50,000 query rows and 100 callouts per transaction. In Batch Apex, each execute call is its own transaction, so these limits reset every chunk, and that's why batch can handle millions of records overall. Say a synchronous process needs about 150 queries and fails on the 100 limit. Moving it to a Queueable gives it room up to 200. But if the real cause is a query inside a loop, it will just fail again with more data. So async helps, but it doesn't remove the need for bulkified code. If someone proposes going async just to dodge a limit, I ask them to show me the query count first.
points: SOQL: 100 sync, 200 async
Heap: 6 MB sync, 12 MB async
CPU: 10 s sync, 60 s async
DML, query rows and callout limits stay the same

So my pattern is: set up data, call startTest, enqueue the job or do the DML that fires it, call stopTest, and then query and assert. For example, if inserting an Account kicks off a Queueable that sets its Rating, I insert the Account between startTest and stopTest, and right after stopTest I query it and assert the Rating is set. For batch tests, only one execute runs, so I create no more test records than the scope size. Queueable chaining is restricted in tests, so I guard the chaining code. For callouts, I call Test.setMock with an HttpCalloutMock right after startTest, before the code that calls out.

a: The trigger enqueues one async job per record, and that's the bug. A data load sends records in chunks of 200, so the trigger tries to make 200 future calls, and the limit is 50 per transaction, giving the Too many future calls error. The fix is to collect all relevant Ids in the trigger and make one async call for the whole batch. I would also switch to a Queueable that takes the full Id set, and if the work per record is heavy, the Queueable can process a slice and chain the rest. I would also check whether the code is already running in async context with System.isFuture or System.isBatch to avoid illegal nested calls. To stop it coming back, I'd make a 200-record bulk test a standard for every trigger, because that catches this before any data load does.

q: How would you design async processing for a high-volume integration in Salesforce?
alt: Design an async architecture for thousands of updates per hour
How do you avoid hitting async limits at scale?
Best practices for asynchronous design in a large org
a: I'd design it by separating capture from processing. Triggers stay thin. They only detect changes and either publish a platform event or write a lightweight staging record. The processing then happens in bulk, through a platform event trigger, a Queueable that handles a slice and chains the rest, or a scheduled batch for big backlogs. Say we're sending order updates to an ERP. The Order trigger just writes a staging row with status Pending. A Queueable picks up a slice of Pending rows, sends them, marks them Sent, and chains the next slice. I keep jobs idempotent and re-runnable, and that status field means a record is never processed twice. For failures, I add finalizers or BatchApexErrorEvent. I watch the org-wide daily async execution limit and the five concurrent batch slots, and I don't launch batches from triggers. Monitoring through AsyncApexJob and an error log object completes the design. The trade-off I'd explain to stakeholders is a little latency, a few seconds to minutes, in exchange for a sync that recovers on its own.

If the job stops halfway, I just run it again and it picks up the rest. Callout limits apply per execute, so each chunk can make up to 100 callouts, and the total callout time is limited too. That's why I set a small scope that matches how many callouts each record needs, or I send one bulk request per chunk if the API supports it. For example, if each record needs two callouts, the default scope of 200 would need 400 calls, so I'd drop the scope to something like 40. I use a Named Credential for the endpoint and authentication. And callouts have to happen before any DML in the same execute, so I collect all the responses first and then update the records with their sync status at the end. a: I chain from finish, because that's the only point where I know the first job is done. I start the second batch from the finish method of the first one. Finish only runs after all chunks are complete, so that guarantees the order. If the second job depends on success, I query AsyncApexJob in finish and only chain if there were no errors, or I pass a flag. For example, batch one recalculates Account totals, and batch two builds summary records from those totals. In batch one's finish, I check that NumberOfErrors is zero, and then I call Database.executeBatch on batch two. For longer pipelines, I sometimes pass a parameter into a generic batch so it knows which step to run next. If the second step is small, I can enqueue a Queueable from finish instead. q: Write a batch to delete records older than two years.

Clean up old data automatically every month

a: I'd do this with a scheduled batch. I write a batch whose start query picks records with CreatedDate older than the cutoff, using a date literal like LAST_N_YEARS or a computed Date variable. In execute, I call Database.delete with allOrNone false, so locked or protected records don't fail the whole chunk. Here's the gotcha: deleted records go to the Recycle Bin. They don't count toward storage, but they still sit in the database and slow down queries until they're purged. So I call Database.emptyRecycleBin on the same chunk. Say we're clearing out old Task records. Before deleting anything, I get the retention policy signed off by the business, and if needed I archive the data to an external store or a Big Object first. Then I schedule the batch to run monthly.

q: You need to process 50,000+ records. Would you use Batch or Queueable?

Can queueable process 100k records?
Why not use queueable for millions of records?
when should I pick batch over queueable
a: For 50,000 records or more, I'd go with Batch Apex, and that's the line I give the team. A single Queueable is one transaction, so it can retrieve at most 50,000 rows and process 10,000 DML rows, and everything shares one set of CPU and heap limits. Batch Apex splits the work into chunks, each with fresh limits. A QueryLocator can feed it up to 50 million records, and it's restartable and easy to monitor per chunk. For example, updating 80,000 Cases in one Queueable would hit the 10,000 DML row limit long before it finished. In a batch, that's 400 chunks of 200, each one well within limits. Queueable can be chained to process slices, but then I have to manage the cursor and the chain myself. So Queueable for smaller, more dynamic work, and Batch for large, query-driven volumes.

a: I'd find out where the time goes before changing anything. First I check the Apex Jobs page and AsyncApexJob to see whether it's slow in start or in execute, and whether other batches are queuing ahead of it. A slow start usually means a non-selective query on a growing object. So I check the query plan and add a filter on an indexed field, or request a custom index. A slow execute usually comes from triggers, flows and rollups firing on every DML. So I review the automation on that object and look at debug logs for CPU hotspots. For example, someone may have added a new record-triggered flow on that object, and now it runs for every record in every chunk. I also check for row-lock retries caused by data skew, and tune the scope size. Finally, I filter out records that are already processed, so the job only works on the delta. Going forward, I'd want new automation on high-volume objects reviewed against the batches that touch them, because this kind of slowdown usually comes from an unrelated change.

q: Your batch fails with UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW errors. How do you fix it?

Unable to lock row while batch is running

a: I'd start by finding which parent records the chunks are fighting over. Row locks in batch usually happen when parallel chunks, or other processes, update records that share the same parent. For example, updating Contacts or Opportunities locks the parent Account, and if many children of one Account are spread across chunks, those chunks compete for the same lock. My fixes are: order the start query by the parent Id so children of the same parent land in the same chunk, reduce the scope size, avoid running the batch at the same time as integrations or data loads, and check for data skew where one parent has thousands of children. I also make the batch re-runnable so failed chunks can simply be picked up again. If skew is the root cause, I raise it as a data model issue with the business, because no amount of tuning fixes one Account with thousands of children.

alt: Prevent overlapping batch runs
Check if a batch is already running before starting
Two instances of the same batch running at once
avoid duplicate batch execution
a: I'd guard it in two places, the scheduler and the data. In the scheduler's execute method, before calling executeBatch, I query AsyncApexJob for my batch class with a status of Holding, Queued, Preparing or Processing. If one exists, I skip this run, or log it, instead of starting a second copy. I filter by ApexClass.Name and JobType BatchApex. Why it matters: say the hourly sync batch normally takes 20 minutes, but one day it takes 90. Without this check, the next run starts while the first one is still going, and two copies of the same batch can process the same records twice and cause lock errors. a: That's almost always state growing chunk after chunk. With Database.Stateful, instance variables are carried between chunks and serialized every time. So if I keep adding records to a list or map, the state keeps growing, and eventually it goes past the 12 MB async heap, usually late in the job. That's why it fails near the end and not at the start. Say I'm saving every processed Account into a stateful list so I can report on them in finish. It's fine at chunk 10, but by chunk 400 that list is huge. The fix is to keep only what's really needed, like counters, totals or a capped number of error messages, not whole sObjects. If I need detailed results, I write them to a custom log object inside execute instead of holding them in memory. And if the totals can be worked out later with an aggregate query, removing Stateful entirely also speeds the job up. In review, any Stateful batch that collects sObjects gets a question from me.

q: What is the difference between SOQL and SOSL?

a: I use SOQL when I know where the data lives, and SOSL when I'm searching for text. SOQL queries one object at a time, plus its related objects, with precise filters, like a SQL SELECT. I use it when I know which object the data is in, for example all open Opportunities for an Account. SOSL is a text search across multiple objects at once using the search index, like a global search. I use it when I have a search term and do not know which object or field it is in, for example searching a name across Accounts, Contacts and Leads. SOQL returns a list of records; SOSL returns a list of lists, one per object. SOSL has a limit of 20 searches per transaction and returns at most 2,000 results. In review, the thing I watch for is SOSL being used where a filtered SOQL would be more precise.

a: I'd use a subquery, so I get parents and children in one go. A parent-to-child query uses a nested SELECT inside the field list. Inside it, I use the child relationship name, which is plural, like Contacts for standard objects, or the name ending in __r for custom ones, like Invoices__r. Each parent record then comes back with a list of its children that I can loop over. For example, SELECT Name, (SELECT LastName FROM Contacts) FROM Account gives me each Account with its Contacts attached. That saves queries, because I get parents and children in one SOQL instead of querying in a loop. If you're not sure of the child relationship name, it's shown on the lookup field definition. And the subquery can have its own WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Querying children in a loop is something I always flag in code review.

q: How do you prevent SOQL injection in dynamic SOQL?
alt: What is SOQL injection?
How to use String.escapeSingleQuotes?
Safe way to build a dynamic query from user input
dynamic soql security
a: My rule is simple: user input never goes into a query string unbound. SOQL injection happens when user input is glued straight into a dynamic query string, so a crafted value can change the query logic and expose data. Say a search box builds the WHERE clause by adding whatever the user typed inside quotes. If they type a quote followed by an OR condition, they can pull back records they shouldn't see. The best defence is bind variables. In Database.query I reference a local variable with a colon, and the value is treated as data, never as query syntax. Where I can't bind, like a field name or sort direction, I check against an allowlist, for example confirming the field exists in the object's describe. String.escapeSingleQuotes is a fallback for string values. And I run the query in user mode so it respects the user's access. Any string concatenation in dynamic SOQL gets flagged in review, and I'd have a static code scan check for it too.
points: Never concatenate raw user input
Use bind variables in Database.query

The map keys match the names after the colon in the query. For example, the query says WHERE Industry = :industry, and I pass a map with the key "industry" set to "Banking". The third parameter is an AccessLevel, and I usually pass USER_MODE. It keeps the safety of bind variables, so it's a clean way to avoid injection.

q: What is a selective query and which fields are indexed?
alt: What makes a SOQL query selective?
Which fields are indexed by default in Salesforce?
How do indexes work in Salesforce?
non selective query error
a: Selectivity is what keeps queries working as data grows. A selective query is one where the WHERE clause filters on an indexed field and narrows the results enough that Salesforce can use the index instead of scanning the whole table. Fields indexed by default include Id, Name, OwnerId, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp, RecordTypeId, lookup and master-detail fields, and fields marked External Id or Unique. For other fields, Salesforce Support can create a custom index. Selectivity matters most on large objects. In triggers, a non-selective query on an object with more than about 200,000 records can throw a non-selective query error. For example, a trigger filtering Cases on an unindexed custom text field might work fine in a small sandbox, then fail in production once there are a million Cases. Filters like not equals, leading wildcards, or comparing with null often stop the index from being used. That's why I ask for trigger queries to be checked against production-sized data, not just a small sandbox.
points: Filter on an indexed field that narrows results
Default indexes: Id, Name, OwnerId, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp, RecordTypeId, lookups, External Id, Unique
Custom indexes via Salesforce Support
Avoid !=, leading %, null filters on big objects

q: What are the selectivity thresholds for standard and custom indexes?
alt: When does the optimizer use an index in Salesforce?
Selectivity threshold percentages
How does the query optimizer decide between index and table scan?
a: These numbers decide whether your index helps at all. The query optimizer only uses an index if the filter returns a small enough share of the object's records. For a standard index, the threshold is 30 percent of the first million records and 15 percent of records beyond that, up to a maximum of one million. For a custom index, it's 10 percent of the first million and 5 percent beyond that, up to 333,333 records. So say an object has 500,000 records. A filter on a standard indexed field has to return under 150,000 rows, and on a custom indexed field under 50,000. If it's expected to return more, the optimizer does a full table scan. With AND conditions, the combined filter can be selective even if each field alone isn't. With OR, every condition has to be indexed and selective. And records in the Recycle Bin count too. When a stakeholder asks why a filter is slow, this is the threshold I walk them through.
points: Standard index: 30% of first 1M, 15% after, max 1M
Custom index: 10% of first 1M, 5% after, max 333,333
Above threshold means full table scan
OR needs every condition indexed

To turn it on, I go to Help, Preferences, and switch on Enable Query Plan. Then a Query Plan button shows up in the Query Editor. It lists the possible plans with the leading operation type, like Index, TableScan or Sharing, the fields used, the estimated cardinality, and a relative cost. A cost below 1 means the plan is selective. Say a list view on Cases is slow. I paste its query in, click Query Plan, and see that the best plan is a TableScan with a cost above 1. That tells me to rewrite the filter to use indexed fields, add a more selective condition, or ask Support for a custom index. I'd like the team to run it on new queries against large objects before they reach review.

q: What are skinny tables?
alt: Explain skinny tables in Salesforce
How to speed up reports on a huge object?
When should you request a skinny table?
a: Skinny tables are a late-stage option, not a first fix. A skinny table is a special table that Salesforce Support creates for a large object, holding a subset of the fields people use most. Normally Salesforce joins standard and custom field storage behind the scenes. A skinny table avoids those joins, and it leaves out soft-deleted rows, so reports, list views and queries on those fields run faster. It's kept in sync automatically. Say an Opportunity object has 20 million records and the pipeline report always uses the same eight fields. A skinny table with those eight fields is exactly the use case. The limitations: it's enabled only through Support, it can't include fields from other objects, and if you need new fields in it, you contact Support again. I only look at it after indexing and query tuning, for objects with millions of records where reporting is slow.

q: How do you handle large data volumes in Salesforce?
alt: What are LDV best practices?
Org has hundreds of millions of records, how to keep it fast?
Large data volume strategy
ldv considerations salesforce
a: I handle large data volumes in layers, and I plan for them before go-live rather than after. First, data model and queries: selective filters on indexed fields, custom indexes from Support, and skinny tables for heavy reporting objects. Second, store less: archive old data to an external store or Big Objects, and purge logs on a schedule. Third, avoid data skew, so keep the number of children per parent and records per owner reasonable. Fourth, loading: use Bulk API, defer sharing calculations during big loads, and temporarily turn off non-essential automation. Fifth, sharing: a simpler role hierarchy and public read where possible keep the sharing tables smaller. For example, if the Case object holds years of closed Cases that nobody opens anymore, I'd archive the old ones to a Big Object and keep only recent ones live. Finally, I monitor with the query plan and test with realistic volumes in a full sandbox. The archive rules need business sign-off, so I bring that conversation in early.

Archive with Big Objects or external storage
Avoid account, ownership and lookup skew
Bulk API and deferred sharing for loads
Test with realistic volumes

q: What is data skew and what are its types?
alt: Explain account data skew
What is ownership skew and lookup skew?
Why are too many child records under one parent a problem?
data skew in salesforce
a: Data skew is a design risk I look for early. It's when too many records are tied to one parent or one owner, roughly more than 10,000. There are three types. Account data skew is one Account with a huge number of child records, like Contacts or Opportunities. Updating children locks the parent, so you get record lock errors, and sharing recalculation gets slow. A classic case is a catch-all Account, something like "Unassigned", with 50,000 Contacts parked on it. Ownership skew is when one user owns a very large number of records of an object, often an integration user. Changing that user's role or the sharing model triggers heavy sharing recalculation. Lookup skew is when a very large number of records look up to the same record, which causes lock contention on inserts and updates. The fix in each case is to spread the children or ownership across more parents or users. I'd rather catch it in the data model review than in a production lock error.
points: Roughly more than 10,000 records on one parent or owner
Account skew: lock errors, slow sharing
Ownership skew: sharing recalculation pain
Lookup skew: lock contention on one lookup target

q: An integration user owns two million records and changing its role takes hours. How do you fix it?
alt: Ownership skew problem with integration user
Sharing recalculation is very slow for one user
One user owns too many records, best practice
integration user owns all records
a: This is ownership skew, and I'd fix the design, not just the timing. When a user who owns millions of records moves in the role hierarchy, Salesforce has to recalculate sharing for all of them, and that's why it takes hours. If the integration user really has to own the records, I put it in a role at the top of the hierarchy, or give it no role at all, so its records don't roll up to a lot of managers. And I never change that user's role during business hours. Better still, I spread ownership across real users or queues based on business rules. For example, records coming in through the integration get assigned by territory or region, instead of all staying with the integration user. Also, if the object's sharing is Public Read/Write, most of the sharing cost goes away, so I check whether a private model is really needed. That's a trade-off I'd take to the business, because opening up sharing is a security decision, not just a performance one.
points: Ownership skew drives heavy sharing recalculation
Keep the owner with no role or a top-level isolated role
Distribute ownership across users or queues
Review whether a private sharing model is needed

q: What does FOR UPDATE do in SOQL?
alt: How do you lock records in Apex?
Explain record locking with SOQL
Prevent two users updating the same record at the same time
for update keyword soql
a: I use FOR UPDATE when two users could change the same value at once. Adding FOR UPDATE to a SOQL query locks the returned records for the rest of the transaction. No other transaction can update them until mine commits or rolls back. Others wait, and if the lock isn't released within about ten seconds, they get an UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW error. I use it for things like counters, invoice number generation or inventory. Say two users place orders at the same moment for the last 5 units of a product. Without a lock, both read 5, both subtract, and the stock ends up wrong. With FOR UPDATE, the second one waits until the first finishes, then reads the real value. One rule: you can't use ORDER BY with FOR UPDATE. And I keep locked transactions short and only lock the records I really need. In review, I check that nothing slow or heavy runs while the lock is held.
points: Locks returned rows until the transaction ends
Prevents lost updates in race conditions
Other transactions wait, then may get UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW
Cannot combine with ORDER BY

q: Users get UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW errors during a data load. How do you troubleshoot it?
alt: Unable to lock row error, what causes it?
Record currently unavailable error in Salesforce
How to fix lock errors when loading child records?
unable to lock row fix
a: I'd treat it as a load-design problem first, not a code problem. UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW means a transaction waited too long for a record that another one had locked. During loads, the usual cause is parallel batches updating children of the same parent, because inserting or updating a child locks its parent, or a rollup summary updating the same parent. Say I'm loading Opportunities and a few big Accounts have thousands each. If those rows are spread across parallel batches, they all fight over the same Account. So my steps are: sort the load file by the parent Id so one parent's children land in the same batch, switch the Bulk API job to serial mode if needed, reduce batch size, and check for data skew. I also look for triggers or flows that update one common record, like a single settings record, and I schedule loads outside integration and batch windows. In code, a short retry can help for transient locks. I make the sorted-by-parent rule part of the team's load checklist, so it doesn't depend on who runs the load.
points: Parallel batches lock the same parent
Sort by parent Id; use serial mode or smaller batches
Check rollups, triggers and data skew
Avoid overlapping jobs; retry transient failures

q: What is the query rows limit and how do you avoid 'Too many query rows: 50001'?
alt: Too many query rows 50001 error fix
How many records can SOQL return in Apex?
Query rows governor limit
fifty thousand rows limit
a: The fix is to fetch less, or move the work to batch. In one transaction, all SOQL queries together can retrieve at most 50,000 records, sync or async. Go over that and you get Too many query rows 50001. To avoid it, I tighten filters so I only fetch what I need, use LIMIT where it makes sense, and use aggregate queries like COUNT instead of fetching rows just to count them. For example, if a page only needs to show how many open Cases an Account has, I run a COUNT query instead of pulling back every Case record. If I really do need to process more than 50,000 records, I move the work into Batch Apex with a QueryLocator, which can handle up to 50 million. I also check that a query in a trigger isn't accidentally pulling a whole table, which is exactly the kind of thing I look for in review.
points: 50,000 rows total per transaction
Tighter filters and LIMIT
Use COUNT() instead of fetching rows to count
Batch Apex for larger volumes

q: How do you fix 'Too many SOQL queries: 101'?
alt: SOQL inside a for loop problem
System.LimitException too many SOQL queries
How to bulkify a query in a trigger?
101 soql error
a: Nine times out of ten it's a query inside a loop, and bulkifying fixes it. This error means the transaction ran more than 100 SOQL queries in synchronous context. Almost always it is a query inside a loop, for example querying the Account for every Contact in a trigger, which fails as soon as 101 records come in. The fix is to bulkify: collect the Ids in a Set first, run one query outside the loop with IN, store the results in a Map by Id, and then look up from the map inside the loop. I also check for recursion, where a trigger fires again and repeats queries, and for multiple automations on the same object adding queries. That last one is why I push for one trigger per object, so the team can see every query that fires.
points: Usually a SOQL query inside a loop
Collect Ids, query once with IN, use a Map
Check trigger recursion and other automation
Limit is 100 sync, 200 async

q: What is the difference between Database.getQueryLocator and Database.query?
alt: When to use getQueryLocator vs a normal query?
Why does batch use a QueryLocator?
Database.query vs Database.getQueryLocator
a: The difference is a loaded list versus a cursor. Database.query runs a dynamic SOQL string right away and returns a list of records, so it's bound by the normal 50,000 query rows limit. Database.getQueryLocator returns a QueryLocator, which is a cursor-like object over the result set, not a loaded list. In Batch Apex start, returning a QueryLocator lets the batch go through up to 50 million records, because records are fetched chunk by chunk. So if a batch has to process 3 million Contacts, start returns Database.getQueryLocator with the query. If I tried to load them with Database.query, it would fail at 50,001 rows. QueryLocators are also used with StandardSetController for pagination in Visualforce. So in normal code I use Database.query or static SOQL, and in batch start I use getQueryLocator.

getQueryLocator: cursor over results

Also used with StandardSetController

q: What are semi-joins and anti-joins in SOQL?

Find accounts that have closed won opportunities in one query
What is NOT IN subquery in SOQL?
semi join anti join soql
a: Semi-joins and anti-joins let me filter on related records without writing loops. A semi-join is a WHERE condition with IN and a subquery, used to return records that have related records matching some criteria, for example Accounts that have at least one closed won Opportunity. An anti-join uses NOT IN with a subquery to return records that do not have such related records, for example Accounts with no Contacts. The subquery must select a single Id or lookup field, and there are restrictions, like not using them inside OR conditions and a limited number per query. They are efficient because the filtering happens in the database, not in Apex loops. When I see code querying children and checking for empty lists, I suggest one of these instead.

q: How do you query polymorphic fields using TYPEOF?

Query WhatId fields on Task with TYPEOF
How to get different fields based on the related object type?
type of soql
a: TYPEOF is the clean way to handle polymorphic fields in one query. A polymorphic field can point to records of different object types. TYPEOF lets me pick which fields to return depending on the actual type of the related record, with a WHEN branch per object and an optional ELSE. Say I'm building an activity timeline from Tasks. q: What is the difference between WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED and WITH USER_MODE?
alt: How do you enforce field level security in SOQL?
Which is better, security enforced or user mode?
Explain USER_MODE in SOQL
FLS in apex queries
a: I'd go with WITH USER_MODE. Both make a SOQL query respect the running user's permissions, because Apex runs in system mode by default. WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks object and field access only for fields in the SELECT and FROM clauses. It throws an exception on the first inaccessible field, and it has gaps, like not supporting traversal of polymorphic fields. WITH USER_MODE is newer, and it's what Salesforce now recommends. It enforces object permissions, field-level security and sharing rules, checks fields in WHERE and ORDER BY too, and can report all inaccessible fields at once. For example, if a user can't see a Salary field and the query only uses it in the WHERE clause, SECURITY_ENFORCED won't check it, but USER_MODE will. WITH USER_MODE is the standard I set for new code, and older SECURITY_ENFORCED queries get moved over when we touch them. And you can't combine both clauses in one query.
points: Apex runs in system mode by default
SECURITY_ENFORCED: SELECT/FROM only, fails on first field
USER_MODE: CRUD, FLS and sharing, all clauses
Salesforce recommends USER_MODE

q: How do you enforce security on DML and dynamic queries?

enforce crud and fls on dml
a: My default is user mode everywhere a user's data is involved. For DML, the Database methods accept an AccessLevel parameter. So Database.insert with AccessLevel.USER_MODE checks the user's object and field permissions and sharing before saving. The same works for Database.query and Database.queryWithBinds. For inline DML there's the as user keyword, like insert as user. Sometimes I'd rather quietly drop the fields a user can't see than throw an error. For example, say an LWC lists Contacts, and some users don't have access to a sensitive custom field. Before returning the data, I run Security.stripInaccessible, which gives me copies of the records without the inaccessible fields, so the component still loads for everyone. And classes should be declared with sharing, so record-level sharing applies. A class without an explicit sharing keyword doesn't get through my review.

q: What is the Bulk API and when do you use it?

a: Bulk API is my choice once volume goes past a few thousand records. It's built for loading or extracting large numbers of records asynchronously. Instead of sending records one request at a time, you submit a job with CSV data, and Salesforce processes it in batches in the background. Bulk API 2.0 is the simpler version. You create a job, upload the data, and Salesforce handles the batching for you. For small, real-time updates, REST or the Composite API is a better fit. Agreeing that split with the integration team early saves a lot of rework.

q: What is the difference between Data Loader and Data Import Wizard?

q: What is an External ID and how does upsert work?
alt: Explain upsert in Salesforce
Why do we use external Id fields?
How to avoid duplicates when loading data from another system?
upsert using external id apex
a: Every integrated object on my teams gets an External ID, because it's what makes upsert safe. An External ID is a custom field marked as an external identifier, holding the record's Id from another system, like an ERP. It's indexed automatically. Upsert uses a key field to decide, per record, whether to insert or update. If a record with that External ID value exists, it's updated. If not, a new one is created. If more than one matches, that record fails. Say the ERP sends customer C-1001 every night. The first night it gets created in Salesforce. Every night after that, the same record just gets updated, with no duplicates, and I never need to know its Salesforce Id. That's what makes integrations and repeat loads safe. In Apex I use Database.upsert with the field token, and in Data Loader I pick the External ID field as the match key.

Indexed automatically
Upsert: match then update, else insert

q: What is a SOQL for loop and when should you use it?
alt: How to avoid heap size errors when querying many records?

a: I use a SOQL for loop when a query can return a lot of rows and heap is the worry. It runs the query right inside the for statement, and Salesforce fetches the records in batches of 200 behind the scenes, instead of loading everything into memory at once. That keeps heap usage low when a query returns a lot of records. I can go one record at a time, or use the list form to get 200 records per iteration. The list form is better when I'm doing DML, because I can update each chunk. Say a query returns 20,000 Contacts. A normal list holds all 20,000 in heap. With the list form of the for loop, I hold 200 at a time and update each group. It doesn't raise the 50,000 query rows limit, though, it only helps with heap. And I still never put a query or DML inside the inner per-record loop.

Reduces heap usage

q: A trigger query fails with 'Non-selective query against large object type'. How do you fix it?
alt: Non selective query error in trigger

Query works in sandbox but fails in production with large data
how to make my query selective
a: I'd fix the filter so it can use an index. This error is thrown in triggers when a query on an object with a large number of records, roughly over 200,000, can't use an index and would need a full table scan. It often works in sandbox and fails in production, just because of the data size. To fix it, I add a filter on an indexed field, like an Id set, a lookup, CreatedDate, or an External ID field, and make sure that filter is selective. I remove patterns that block indexes, like not equals, leading wildcards, or null checks on custom fields. For example, a trigger that queries Cases where a custom Region field is not null will scan the table. Filtering by the AccountIds from the trigger records instead uses the lookup index. If the business filter has to be on a custom field, I ask Salesforce Support for a custom index, and I check the result with the Query Plan tool. Because it only shows up at production volume, I ask the team to think about selectivity whenever a trigger query touches a big object.

Avoid !=, leading %, null on custom fields

q: What are date literals in SOQL?
alt: SOQL query for records created this month
How to filter by last 30 days in SOQL?
What is LAST_N_DAYS in SOQL?
date functions in soql
a: I prefer date literals over date maths in Apex wherever they fit. They're keywords for relative date ranges, so I don't have to calculate dates in Apex. Common ones are TODAY, YESTERDAY, THIS_WEEK, LAST_MONTH, THIS_QUARTER, THIS_YEAR, LAST_N_DAYS with a number, and NEXT_N_DAYS. For example, WHERE CloseDate = NEXT_N_DAYS:30 gives me Opportunities closing in the next 30 days, and the same query keeps working tomorrow without any change. They're evaluated in the running user's time zone. For datetime fields like CreatedDate, the literal covers the full day range, so CreatedDate = TODAY catches everything from midnight to midnight. There are also date functions like CALENDAR_YEAR or CALENDAR_MONTH that I use with GROUP BY for reports, for example counting records per month. The time zone point is the one I remind people about, because it explains a lot of "missing record" complaints.

Evaluated in the user's time zone
Date functions like CALENDAR_MONTH with GROUP BY

q: You need a list of Accounts that have no open Cases. How would you query it?

a: I'd use an anti-join, which filters in the database instead of looping in Apex. The query selects Accounts where Id is NOT IN a subquery of AccountId from Case where IsClosed is false. The alternative of querying all Accounts with a Cases subquery and checking for empty lists in Apex uses many more query rows and heap. In review, this is a pattern I steer people towards whenever I see empty-list checks on subquery results.

q: How do you query deleted or archived records with ALL ROWS?
alt: How to get records from the recycle bin in SOQL?
What is ALL ROWS in Apex?
Query IsDeleted records
undelete records using apex
a: ALL ROWS is how I reach records in the Recycle Bin, because by default SOQL doesn't return them. In Apex, adding ALL ROWS at the end of the query includes deleted records, and I can filter with IsDeleted equals true to get only those. It also returns archived Activities. Say a user deletes 30 Contacts by mistake. I can query them with ALL ROWS and IsDeleted = true, then run the undelete DML statement on that list to bring them back. It's also handy for auditing. A couple of rules: ALL ROWS can't be combined with FOR UPDATE, and through the API the equivalent is the queryAll operation. And once records are purged from the Recycle Bin, you can't get them back this way. So when someone reports an accidental delete, I tell them to raise it fast, before the bin is emptied.

Filter with IsDeleted = true
Use with undelete to restore
Not allowed with FOR UPDATE

q: How do you paginate SOQL results?
alt: What is OFFSET in SOQL?
How to implement pagination in an LWC data table?
LIMIT and OFFSET in SOQL
server side pagination salesforce
a: For small lists, OFFSET is fine, but for anything large I'd go with keyset pagination. The simple way is LIMIT with OFFSET. LIMIT sets the page size, OFFSET skips the earlier rows, and ORDER BY keeps the order stable. The catch is that OFFSET maxes out at 2,000 rows, so it doesn't work for deep pages, and large offsets get slower. For bigger data sets I use keyset pagination. I remember the last record's sort value and Id, and the next page's query filters for values greater than that. Say I show 50 Accounts per page, sorted by Name. Page 41 needs an OFFSET of 2,000, which is the maximum, so page 42 breaks. With keyset, I just ask for Accounts that sort after the last one I showed, which works at any depth and uses the index. For a total count to show page numbers, I run a separate COUNT query.
points: LIMIT plus OFFSET with ORDER BY
OFFSET maximum is 2,000
Keyset pagination for large data
Separate COUNT() for totals

q: You need to migrate ten million records from a legacy system into Salesforce. How would you plan it?
alt: Plan a large data migration to Salesforce
Data migration strategy for millions of records
Steps for migrating data with relationships
how to load 10 million records
a: I'd plan it in phases, and I'd agree the cutover and rollback plan with the business before any data moves. First, mapping and cleansing. I map legacy fields to Salesforce, deduplicate, and add an External ID field on each object for the legacy key. Second, load order. Users and reference data first, then parents like Accounts, then children like Contacts and Opportunities, linking them through External IDs with upsert. So a Contact row just carries its legacy account key, and upsert finds the right Account. Third, performance. Use Bulk API 2.0 through Data Loader or an ETL tool, temporarily disable or bypass non-essential triggers, flows and validation rules, defer sharing calculations, and sort children by parent to avoid lock errors. Fourth, testing. I do a full-size run in a full sandbox first. Then, after the production load, I reconcile record counts and check sample data, so I know ten million in the source really landed as ten million in Salesforce. I want that reconciliation signed off by the data owners, not just by the team that ran the load.
points: Cleanse data and add External IDs
Load parents before children, upsert by External ID
Bulk API, bypass automation, defer sharing
Sort by parent to reduce lock errors
Rehearse in full sandbox, reconcile after
